slides.text: A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a pointer to the next node, and the last one points to nil. You will build, walk, change and reverse them with the pointers you already know.
The nodes are not side by side like a slice. You reach one only by following pointers from the **head**, the first node. The sketch is not Go.
A node needs a field that points to another node of the same type. That works with a pointer: a node cannot contain a whole node of its own type, but it can point to one.
To visit every node, keep a pointer to the current one and hop until it is nil. The snippet is pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
current = head
while current is not nil
    use current
    current = current.next

slides.text: Adding in front only needs the new node to point at the old head. Adding at the end means finding the last node first, unless the list also keeps a pointer to it.
Order matters when linking in the middle: the new node must take the old next node **before** the old one is pointed at it, or the rest of the list is lost. Pseudo code, not Go.

slides.text: A search returns a pointer to the node itself, so changing it changes the list. Nil means there was no match, and callers must check for it.

To remove a node, the node before it skips over it. Nothing points at the removed node afterward, and Go frees it on its own. The head has no node before it, so it is a special case. Pseudo code, not Go.

slides.text: Reversing walks the list once, pointing each node at the one before it. The next node must be saved before its link changes, or the walk loses its place. Pseudo code, not Go.
slides.code:
previous = nil
while node is not nil
    saved = node.next
    node.next = previous
    previous = node
    node = saved

slides.text: A node with a pointer back to its previous node is a doubly linked list. A stack can sit on a list by using the head as the top. Two pointers moving at different speeds find the middle in one pass.

exercises.title: A stack on a list
exercises.guide: Push and pop at the head of a list.

chunks.guide: Pushing is adding to the front: the head is the top.
Popping is removing the head. An empty stack has nothing to give.
Last in, first out. The third pop finds it empty.
chunks.text:
var stack Stack
    stack.Push(1)
    stack.Push(2)
    value, ok := stack.Pop()
    fmt.Println(value, ok)
    stack.Pop()
    _, ok = stack.Pop()
    fmt.Println(ok)
